messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Johnson is a 68-year-old widowed African man who has been a dancer for most of his life. Tragically, he was involved in a life-threatening motor vehicle collision several months ago. Since the accident, Mr. Johnson's life has been marked by a pervasive sense of unease and fragmented memories. On the day of the collision, Mr. Johnson was on his way to a dance rehearsal when another car swerved into his lane, causing a severe crash. The impact was jarring, and he remembers feeling disoriented and overwhelmed with fear as sirens approached. Despite receiving medical attention, the trauma has left deep emotional scars. Mr. Johnson struggles most with incomplete memories of the event. He feels like only parts of what happened are accessible to him, and when he tries to recall it deliberately, the memory is elusive. This difficulty in remembering leaves him feeling lost and confused about his own experience, which fuels his self-doubt. "I can't trust that I will do the right thing," he often tells himself. His body feels unreliable too; the collision left him with lingering pain and a sense of vulnerability. The fragmented nature of Mr. Johnson's memory has also influenced his maladaptive strategies. He avoids going out, preferring to stay at home where he feels safer. Even when he does venture outside, he finds it difficult to socialize with people he once enjoyed spending time with. The fear that he can't trust himself or his body makes him reluctant to engage in activities that were once a part of his daily routine. This self-doubt and sense of institutional failure (feeling let down by the systems meant to protect him) exacerbate his fears. When something takes longer than expected, Mr. Johnson assumes the worst is happening, putting him on high alert for any unexpected sounds or events that could trigger a flashback. "I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room," he admits. Mr. Johnson's threat perceptions have become deeply intertwined with his maladaptive strategies. He avoids therapy content because discussing it makes him feel more vulnerable and unsure of how to proceed safely in the world. This avoidance reinforces his negative appraisals, creating a self-perpetuating cycle where each layer of fear feeds into another. Over time, Mr. Johnson’s life has become increasingly circumscribed by these fears. His occupation as a dancer is particularly affected; he can no longer participate in performances or rehearsals without intense anxiety. When he does attempt to go out, the slightest delay or unexpected sound triggers his hypervigilance, making it difficult for him to engage meaningfully with others. What frightens Mr. Johnson most is the uncertainty and lack of control over his own memories and experiences. He fears that he will never fully understand what happened and whether he can trust himself again. However, his current state has pushed him to seek help, driven by a hope that therapy might provide some clarity and a way to reclaim parts of his life. In conclusion, Mr. Johnson’s struggle is one of fragmented memories and overwhelming fears, where each layer of trauma feeds into the next, creating a complex web of negative appraisals, maladaptive strategies, and heightened threat perceptions. His journey to recovery will involve addressing these interwoven layers in a way that allows him to regain trust in himself and his experiences.
